problem: Imitation-learning image-goal navigation policies suffer from causal confusion: they over-rely on the current observation and ignore the goal image. Monocular scale uncertainty and complex outdoor environments make this worse.
motivation: Outdoor monocular image-goal navigation without a map needs the policy to actually use the goal image, otherwise it fails to reach the goal. The authors observe that training with variable-length autoregressive waypoint sequences forces stronger dependence on the goal image.
key_idea: ArMoNa: a pre-trained 3D vision model encodes the current and goal images into fusion features, and an autoregressive decoder emits discrete waypoints token by token until an end token, so variable-length waypoint training strengthens the causal link between the goal image and the actions.
insight: The abstract says that variable-length autoregressive waypoint training increases attention to the goal image, which reduces causal confusion. It also says a pre-trained 3D vision encoder helps with monocular scale uncertainty and cross-camera generalization, for example to mobile phones. No ablation numbers are available because only the abstract was provided.
method: Observation encoder: a pre-trained 3D vision model encodes the current image and the goal image, which are randomly selected during training, into fusion features.
Autoregressive action decoder: generates discrete waypoint tokens conditioned on the fusion features.
Variable-length waypoint training: the decoder is trained on sequences of varying length, which enhances attention to the goal image and mitigates causal confusion.
Deployment inference: a start token is fed to the decoder, which loops to predict the next waypoint until an end token appears.

setting.backbone: pre-trained 3D vision model encoder + autoregressive transformer decoder (trained)
setting.training_data: not stated in the abstract (imitation learning on image-goal navigation data)
setting.simulator: not stated (simulated environments plus real world)

results: The abstract claims the highest navigation success rate compared with state-of-the-art methods in both simulated and real environments. It also claims generalization to different camera devices such as mobile phones. No numbers are given.
limitations: Only the abstract was available, so details on datasets, metrics and ablations are unknown.
Evaluation is limited to outdoor monocular image-goal navigation.
